title: Session 1: Exercises
text: Data (save into data/ in your project): sleepstudy.csv

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
1. Reaction times
One participant, ten trials of a given task, reaction times in ms:

rt <- c(523, 487, 601, 455, 2310, 512, 498, 577, 466, 540)
condition <- c("easy", "hard", "hard", "easy", "hard",
               "easy", "hard", "hard", "easy", "easy")


How many trials? What are the mean, median, min and max?
One trial looks odd. Which one? Use which.max(). Why are the mean and the median so different?
Make rt_clean, without trials over 2000 ms. What is the mean now?
What is the mean for "easy" and for "hard" trials, without the odd one? Drop it from both vectors, so they stay aligned.
Convert rt to seconds.

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
2. Missing trials
A second participant missed two trials:

rt2 <- c(523, NA, 487, 150, 601, 455, 2310, NA, 512, 498)


How many trials are missing, and which ones?
What is the mean without them?
Trials faster than 200 ms or slower than 1500 ms are implausible. How many are there? What proportion of the non-missing trials? The mean of TRUE/FALSE values is a proportion.
Try rt2[rt2 > 200]. Why do NAs appear? Keep only the trials that are present and plausible.

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
3. Spot the bugs
This code has five mistakes. Fix them. One gives no error, just a wrong answer: which one?

scores <- c(12, 15, 9, 20, 17)
group <- c("a", "b", "a", "b", "a")
mean(scores[group = "a"]
maen(scores[group == "b"])
Mean(scores)
summary(Scores)

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
4. A Likert item
Twelve answers to “How often do you have trouble sleeping?”:

answers <- c("often", "never", "sometimes", "always", "often", "rarely",
             "sometimes", "often", "never", "always", "sometimes", "often")


Run table(answers). Does the order make sense?
Make answers_f, an ordered factor from "never" to "always". Run table() again.
as.numeric(answers_f) turns the answers into scores from 1 to 5. What is the mean score?
Someone answers "Often". Add it and rebuild the factor. What happens?

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
6. Your first functions

Write se(), the standard error of the mean, \(s/\sqrt{n}\). Try it on rt_clean.
Now try it on rt2. Make it ignore NAs: sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) and sum(!is.na(x)) help.
Write n_outliers(x, low = 200, high = 1500), which counts the values below low or above high. Try n_outliers(rt2), then n_outliers(rt2, high = 600).

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
7. A drug trial: sleep
sleep comes with R: extra hours of sleep (extra) for 10 patients (ID) under two drugs (group).

Look at it with str(), head() and summary(). How many rows and columns?
What is the mean extra for each drug?
Every patient took both drugs. For each patient, compute drug 2 minus drug 1. How many slept more with drug 2?

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
8. Sleep deprivation: sleepstudy
Reaction times of 18 subjects, one mean per day (Belenky et al., 2003). Days 0 and 1 were training and day 2 is the baseline. After day 2, subjects spent only 3 hours in bed per night.

Read it: sleepstudy <- read.csv(here::here("data", "sleepstudy.csv")).
How many subjects are there?
What is the mean reaction time on day 2, and on day 9?
For each subject, compute the change from day 2 to day 9. Put the two days in two data frames, check that Subject is in the same order, then subtract.
How many subjects slowed down? Who slowed down the most?
Draw a hist() of the changes.

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
9. Your first report

File > New File > Quarto Document. Put your name as author, save it as session1-report.qmd and click Render.
In the header, replace format: html with the lines below and render again. What changed?

format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-location: left

Write a few lines: a ### heading, one bold and one italic word, a short list and a link to a website.

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
10. Bring in your analysis

Copy your exercise 8 code into chunks in the report. Render.
Give the histogram chunk a label and a caption (#| label: fig-change, #| fig-cap: "..."). Refer to it in the text with @fig-change.
Add #| echo: false to the chunk that reads the data. What changes?

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
11. Numbers in the text

Write one sentence with the mean change and the number of subjects who slowed down. Use inline code, as in `{r} round(mean(change))`, never typed numbers.
Copy your sleep code from exercise 7 into the report and complete this sentence:

On average, patients slept `{r} ...` hours more with drug 2 than with drug 1,
and `{r} ...` out of 10 slept more with drug 2.

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
12. Does it render from scratch?

In the console, type x <- 42. In the report, add a chunk with x * 2. Render. What happens, and why?
Delete that chunk, then Session > Restart R and render again. Does everything still work?
Add a last chunk with sessionInfo().

title: Session 1: Exercises
text:
Bonus: PDF and Word

A PDF needs LaTeX. Install TinyTeX once, in the RStudio Terminal (not the Console): quarto install tinytex.
Add two formats to the header:

format:
  html:
    toc: true
    toc-location: left
  pdf: default
  docx: default

Render all three in the Terminal: quarto render session1-report.qmd. Open the PDF and the Word file. What differs from the HTML?

title: Introduction
section: From a sample to general conclusions
text:
From a sample to general conclusions
We observe a tiny portion of the world, e.g. a few subjects, sessions, trials.
We want conclusions that hold in general.

Statistics quantifies how much we can generalise despite

measurement noise (instruments, questionnaires);
variability between and within subjects;
factors we did not measure.

title: Introduction
text:
Aims
Study of populations

100 subjects scanned once: population across individuals.
1 subject scanned daily for a year: population across time.


Study of variation

Variability between subjects, across time, across space.



Data reduction

From millions of numbers per subject to summaries (means, components, features).

Fisher (1925), Statistical Methods for Research Workers, ch. 1

title: Introduction
text:
Pay attention!
Classical tools (t-test, ANOVA, regression) assume independent observations.

Neuroscience data often are not:

10 trials from one subject are more similar than 10 trials from 10 subjects;
the same questionnaire filled in 6 times by one participant gives correlated scores.



Ignoring this leads to overconfidence (underestimation of uncertainty)
A standard tool to deal with correlated responses is mixed models, but we will not cover them in this course.

title: Introduction
text:
The reproducibility crisis

Reproducibility: same data and same analysis give the same results.
Replication: new data on the same question give consistent results.



Nature survey of 1,576 researchers: more than 70% had tried and failed to replicate another scientist’s experiments, more than half their own (Baker, 2016).
70 teams analysed the same brain-imaging data to test the same 9 hypotheses. No two teams used the same workflow, and their results varied considerably (Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020).



Common threats: low statistical power, trying analyses until something is significant (p-hacking), hypotheses made up after seeing the results, unpublished null results, no shared data or code (Munafò et al., 2017).

title: Introduction
text:
A starting point

State the hypothesis before looking at the data.
Share raw data and code. Every number in the paper generated automatically.
Write reports where text, code and results live together.



This is why we analyse data with code.

title: Introduction
text:
Basic R grammar
Run a line: Ctrl+Enter (Windows) / Cmd+Enter (Mac).

a <- 1                    # assign 1 to a (numeric value)
b <- 2
label <- "control"        # character value
a + b

[1] 3



Vectors:

rt <- c(512, 430, 601, 488, 550)  # reaction times (ms)
trials <- 1:5                     # sequence 1 to 5
seq(0, 1, by = 0.25)              # regular sequence

[1] 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00

Working with vectors

rt[1]            # first element

[1] 512

rt[2:4]          # elements 2 to 4

rt / 1000        # convert to seconds

rt - mean(rt)    # centre around the mean

RStudio tips and help

Tab: autocomplete names.
Alt + - / Option + -: insert <-.
Environment pane: the objects you created.
Write code in a file, not the console.



?mean

Read Arguments and Examples. E.g. to ignore NAs in mean(), use na.rm = TRUE.

title: Introduction
text:
Common mistakes
R is case-sensitive: RT and rt are different objects. Pick one style (snake_case: mean_rt).


mean(c(1, 2, 3)

Missing ): R shows + and waits. Press Esc.



maen(rt)

Error in maen(rt) : could not find function "maen"



RT

Error: object 'RT' not found

title: Introduction
text:
Logical values and comparisons



Operator
Meaning
Example




==, !=
equal, not equal
3 == 3 is TRUE


<, >, <=, >=
comparisons
5 > 2 is TRUE


%in%
element in a set
"a" %in% c("a","b") is TRUE


&, |, !
and, or, not
TRUE & FALSE is FALSE





rt <- c(512, 430, 1601, 488, 150)
too_fast_or_slow <- rt < 200 | rt > 1500   # flag implausible trials
rt[!too_fast_or_slow]                       # keep valid trials

[1] 512 430 488

title: Introduction
text:
Factors
Categorical variables with fixed levels:

group <- factor(c("patient", "control", "control", "patient", "control"))
levels(group)

[1] "control" "patient"

table(group)

group
control patient 
      3       2 



Ordered categories (a Likert item):

answer <- c("never", "always", "often", "never")
factor(answer, levels = c("never", "often", "always"), ordered = TRUE)

[1] never  always often  never 
Levels: never < often < always

title: Introduction
text:
Data frames
One row per observation, one column per variable. Columns can have different types.

subjects <- data.frame(
  id    = c("S01", "S02", "S03", "S04"),
  group = factor(c("patient", "control", "patient", "control")),
  age   = c(64, 58, 71, 60),
  score = c(22, 29, 19, 28)
)
subjects

   id   group age score
1 S01 patient  64    22
2 S02 control  58    29
3 S03 patient  71    19
4 S04 control  60    28

Packages

title: Introduction
Introduction
text:
Anatomy of a .qmd file
---
title: "Sleep deprivation: first look"
author: "Your Name"
format: html
---

## Data

```{r}
#| echo: false
sleepstudy <- read.csv(here::here("data", "sleepstudy.csv"))
```

The dataset contains `{r} nrow(sleepstudy)` measurements.

YAML header between ---: title, author, format (html, pdf, docx).
Markdown text: ## Section, **bold**, *italic*, - lists, $\bar x$.
Code chunks: run at render; options start with #|.
Inline code: numbers inside sentences, never typed by hand.

title: Introduction
text:
Rendering and chunk options
Render: Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + K. The file runs from scratch: it must load its own packages and data.








Option
Effect




#| echo: false
hide code, show results


#| eval: false
show code, don’t run it


#| include: false
run, show nothing


#| label: fig-rt and #| fig-cap: "..."
numbered figure, cite with @fig-rt
